clinician.trajectory_summary: A 62-year-old obese female with smoking history, chronic hypertension, hypothyroidism, and recent chemotherapy (gemcitabine/cisplatin 5 months prior) for high-grade urothelial bladder cancer presented with a 3-day history of retrosternal chest pain. On admission, she was hemodynamically stable (BP 110/80 mmHg) without active chest pain. ECG showed normal sinus rhythm with inverted T waves in anterior and lateral leads. Cardiac biomarkers were markedly elevated (troponin I hs 9552 ng/l, BNP 175 pg/ml, NT-proBNP 2691 pg/ml), indicating myocardial injury. Left ventriculography demonstrated akinesis of the apex and apical/mid-anterior wall with reduced ejection fraction of 38%, consistent with apical ballooning. Cardiac catheterization revealed only minor atherosclerotic changes with patent coronary arteries, ruling out acute coronary syndrome. This constellation of findings—acute chest pain, myocardial injury, characteristic apical ballooning on ventriculography, and patent coronaries—confirmed the diagnosis of Takotsubo cardiomyopathy. The patient was qualified for conservative treatment. Hospitalization was uncomplicated without recurrence of chest pain. Follow-up echocardiography demonstrated recovery of left ventricular function with improved ejection fraction of 47%, characteristic of TTS. At discharge, she was prescribed acetylsalicylic acid, bisoprolol, ramipril, atorvastatin, pantoprazole, iron supplementation, and thyroid hormone replacement.
